newsitem.title: USA: Aon profits fall, takes charge for volatile securities.
newsitem.headline: Aon profits fall, takes charge for volatile securities.

text.p: Aon Corp., a leading U.S. insurance broker, said Tuesday it took a $27 million charge after discovering hidden losses from risky securities in the portfolio of an insurance company it acquired earlier this year and authorities are investigating.

Aon, in announcing its second-quarter results, said it took a $27 million charge during the period to account for the loss, which stemmed from "highly volatile" securities in the portfolio of Alexander & Alexander, which it acquired in January for $1.2 billion.
The Chicago-based company said it sold the securities after they were discovered during an audit of the newly acquired company.

Aon Chairman Patrick Ryan said the company was pursuing legal action to try and recover the $27 million. The company also said it is cooperating with law enforcement investigations but declined to say what officials it had contacted.
"This activity was hidden from the management of A&A. Our people did quite a good job of finding it through internal audit," Aon Chairman Patrick Ryan told a conference call.

He said Aon would pursue "legal issues," but declined to say what steps the company might take to recoup the charge. Aon's financial recourse could be limited by the fact it bought A&A from the public with a tender offer.

"The biggest issue frankly from our point of view is we know we got it all," Ryan said. "We're not discounting the value of the $27 million (charge). We'll try to recover it from wherever we have (recourse) ... But we know we've got it."

Including the charge, Aon's earnings fell to $84.2 million, or 48 cents a share, from $86.3 million, or 49 cents a share, in the year-earlier quarter. Revenues rose to $1.42 billion from $932 million.
Excluding the charge, Aon's operating earnings were 58 cents a share, up from 48 cents a year ago.

Mesirow Financial analyst Joanne Smith said she believed the $27 million charge for the securities overshadowed what were otherwise strong results. Aon's brokerage business, she added, turned in "very impressive" results.

Aon Group, Aon's insurance brokerage and consulting services segment, reported 99.7 percent growth in revenues to $923 million, due primarily to major acquisitions. Income before tax and special charges was $127 million, up 123 percent from a year ago.
The insurance underwriting segment posted modest gains, with revenue rising 7 percent to $474 million, it said. Income before tax and special charges rose 6 percent.
Aon shares lost 68.75 cents to $53.5625 i consolidated New York Stock Exchange trading.
Ryan said he did not believe Aon was at risk for fines because of the securities in A&A's portfolio.

Fines could be an issue because the securities included fiduciary funds -- or funds Aon holds on behalf of its customers -- that can only be invested in highly rated, liquid securities, analysts said.

Aon said the probe revealed that A&A held certain highly volatile securities that were incorrectly classified as high-quality money market instruments. Those securities had been carried on A&A's books at inflated values at the time of the acquisition, it said.
